newsitem.title: USA: US lead battery demand set to grow 12 pct by 2002.
newsitem.headline: US lead battery demand set to grow 12 pct by 2002.

text.p: Lead-acid starter battery demand in the United States, the world's biggest market, is set to grow 12 percent between now and the year 2002, Douglas Brown, vice president battery sales at Johnson Controls Battery Group said.
Lead batteries consume over 70 percent of global lead output.

"Despite being a mature industry today, both original equipment and replacement market shipments continue to grow," Brown said in a paper for the Battery Council International meeting in San Diego this week.
Some of the growth will continue from consumers using the wrong sized battery in the car, shortening battery life and the unit is returned.

"The end result of misapplication is an increase in batteries shipped to the retailer, contributing to industry growth, It is uncertain as to how much of the industry growth is due to misapplication," Brown said.
The average age of cars is rising, thereby increasing battery sales. People are also driving further, putting more stress on batteries and reducing normal life.
"Another factor, however, that has lead to the industry growth of battery shipments is the increasing underhood temperatures of cars on the road today," Brown said.
Underhood temperatures are expected to increase to above 225 degrees Fahrenheit by 2002, up from 200 at present. This, along with hotter climates, is shortening battery life.
More people are living in hotter areas of the U.S.
Battery life in the south averages 40 months versus 58 months in the north, studies have shown, Brown said.
New cars are also more loaded with electrical gadgets which put more strain on batteries.

Original equipment battery shipments are expected to continue to rise in 1998 to 16.1 million, in 1999 to 16.5 million, in 2000 to 16.8 million, in 2001 to 17 million, reaching 17.2 million by 2002, up from 15.9 million in 1996.

Replacement battery shipments are expected to grow from 79.9 million in 1996 to 83.1 million in 1998, 85.1 million in 1999, 87.2 million in 2000, 88.9 million in 2001, and 90.7 million units in 2002, Brown said.
Most lead acid batteries are used in cars, with a much smaller amount used in maine, general utility, gold cars and special tractors.
